title: Store the cartons so no stack is taller than three times its base
instruction: Put all five cartons onto the two grey pads, one stack per pad. Each stack's height above its pad must be no more than three times the shorter side of the carton at the bottom of that stack.
context: A common warehouse rule of thumb for hand stacking keeps a free-standing stack no higher than three times the least side of its base, so a tall stack on a narrow base cannot topple onto a worker. One tall stack would be quicker; the robot has to split the cartons and choose which goes at the bottom and how it rests. Done by: hand laborers and freight, stock and material movers.
setup: Two dark grey painted wooden pads (blocks 10 cm x 10 cm, 3 cm tall) are fixed to the table, one 27 cm straight in front of each arm base. Five loose cartons, corrugated cardboard filled to their stated mass, stand on the table between the arms. 14 cm left of the midline, in a row going away from the arms: a blue narrow carton (4 x 4 cm, 9 cm tall, standing on its 4 x 4 cm end, 150 g) 18 cm in front of the arm bases, then two green cube cartons (5 cm on every side, 200 g each) 27 and 36 cm in front. 14 cm right of the midline: two red wide cartons (7 x 7 cm, 4 cm tall, lying on a 7 x 7 cm face, 300 g each) 21 and 33 cm in front. Every carton's sides are square to the table's edges. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Measure from the pad top. A carton rests on a pad when its bottom is within 5 mm of the pad top and its footprint overlaps the pad's 10 x 10 cm top at all, wherever its centre is; it rests on another carton when its bottom is within 5 mm of that carton's top and their footprints overlap. The height limit counts every carton above the pad (its bottom higher than 5 mm below the pad top) whose footprint overlaps the pad or a carton counted in its stack, whether or not it rests there or earns credit. Height limit: 0 overall if, on a pad with a carton resting on it, the highest point of any carton counted in that pad's stack is more than 3 times b above the pad top, b being the shorter footprint side, as it rests, of the carton resting on the pad (the narrowest, if several do): 12 cm with the blue carton standing or lying, 15 cm with a green cube, 21 cm with a red carton lying flat, 12 cm with a red carton on its edge. The same limit applies to cartons stacked on the table: 0 overall if, for any carton whose bottom is within 5 mm of the table top, the cartons counted from it the same way (every carton above the table whose footprint overlaps it or a carton already counted) reach more than 3 times its b above the table top. A stack exactly at its limit passes. Credit: a pad counts nothing unless exactly one carton rests on it, with its centre inside the pad's outline; that carton earns 0.2. Each carton above it earns 0.2 when it rests on the counted carton below with its centre within 15 mm (seen from above) of that carton's centre; counting stops at the first carton that fails. Every counted carton is tilted at most 5 degrees from lying on one of its faces, and is judged as it rests: a carton on its side is allowed. All five counted, both stacks within their limits: 1.0. A carton on the table, on the floor, tipped, or held above the stack (not resting on the pad or a carton) counts nothing; success additionally needs every carton still for 2.5 s.
reset_notes: Stand the five cartons back on their tape marks as in the setup, square to the table edges, the blue one on its end and the red ones on a 7 x 7 cm face; nothing is consumed. The pads stay fixed (screw or tape them down for real trials).
fidelity: Approximate: the cartons are rigid boxes of uniform density, so they don't crush or bulge, and the pads are fixed blocks. Every object has the same rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), grippier than cardboard on wood, so stacks in simulation are somewhat steadier than real ones. The cartons are small stand-ins for shed cartons; the 3:1 ratio scales with them.
